newsitem.title: UK: UK shares end down, upset by Dow's volatile antics.
newsitem.headline: UK shares end down, upset by Dow's volatile antics.

text.p: UK shares ended lower on Wednesday as the antics of the volatile Dow scared investors away and another call for higher interest rates by the Bank of England sent gilts scurrying lower.
The FTSE 100 share index ended 29.9 points lower at 4,207.5, with volume on SEAQ a subdued 715 million shares by 1634 GMT.

Dealers said the market was depressed by Wall Street's recent see-saw performance. The FTSE opened weaker after a 100-point Dow rally evaporated overnight, and although a firmer Dow opening pulled UK shares off their lows in afternoon trade, fears of further volatility continued to worry investors.
"The market is going through a phase of being unsure of itself and a lot of people won't do anything until this uncertainty clears," one dealer said.

"Traders may like volatility but fund managers don't and while the market is behaving like this they won't get involved. People just don't know if they should be buying or selling," he said. "Uncertainty about Wall Street and interest rates here and in the U.S. is keeping people nervous."
Minutes from the UK's December monetary meeting, released on Wednesday, showed continued disagreements between Britain's monetary authorities over interest rates.

Bank of England governor Eddie George said a rate rise of half a percentage point might be needed early this year, but Chancellor Kenneth Clarke disagreed. Economists said Clarke was unlikely to allow rates to rise ahead of the election, which must be held by mid-May.

Weaker-than-expected U.S. December durable goods orders provided support for U.S. Treasuries and helped push the Dow higher. Analysts said the chances of a February U.S. rate rise were also diminishing.
But reasonably bullish fundamentals were not encouraging London investors to buy, dealers said.

"Data on both sides of the Atlantic has been fairly bullish recently," one said. "But although people's heads tell them this is a buying opportunity, their hearts tell them they don't want to be in the market."
Decliners outnumbered gainers by seven to three in the FTSE. Dealers said there had been little pattern to the day's trade.

"Normally you see trends developing in sectors," a trader said. "We don't even have that today -- some stocks are good in any given sector and others have gone in the opposite direction. It's been very stock selective."
Retailer Marks & Spencer was among the day's weakest blue-chip shares, ending down 11p at 482.
Analysts said the company's Christmas trading statement had been reasonable but failed to match optimistic expectations that sent its shares striding higher on Tuesday.
Electronics components supplier Premier Farnell closed 54-1/2p off at 637-1/2, rattled by a late profit warning.

LucasVarity was the FTSE's biggest loser, down 11p or five percent at 209p. Dealers said Tuesday's rise in LucasVarity shares had been overdone, and cautious comments in the Financial Times "Lex" column helped pull the stock lower.
Transport company Stagecoach extended Tuesday's losses, down 38p to 740 after a Merrill Lynch downgrade.

On the upside, First Leisure climbed 18-1/2p to 359-1/2, after naming Michael Grade, who is resigning as chief executive of Channel 4 television, as its executive chairman. It also said it had no plans to buy Rank Group's film distribution arm. Rank shares rose eight pence to 433-1/2.

Retailer WH Smith gained 5-1/2p to 435-1/2 after its first-half profits came in above forecast, and engineering firm TI Group rose 10-1/2p to 549-1/2 after SBC Warburg said the stock was oversold after its recent decline.
-- Andrew Marshall, London newsroom +44 171 542 4367
